questions.stem: A handoff writes a plain `int payload`, then a plain `boolean published`; a reader checks `published`, then reads `payload`. On an x86 build server, 50,000,000 trials with `-Xint` never ended with `published` true and `payload` 0. The same trials with the default flags ended that way 40 times. What explains the difference?

options.text: The JIT can emit the compiled writer's two stores in program order for the processor to swap, since x86 drains buffered stores in order only for interpreted code
options.says: x86 drains one core's buffered stores in order whatever code issued them; the interpreted run showed no swap because nothing reordered the stores before the hardware

options.text: The JIT can emit the compiled writer's two stores out of order, since the JMM lets it reorder stores to different fields
options.says: the reordering disappeared under -Xint and with only C1; the JIT may reorder writes to different fields, which intra-thread semantics allows

options.text: The JIT can keep `payload` in a thread-private copy in the compiled reader, since the JMM lets each thread cache fields until it synchronizes
options.says: caches are coherent; reorderings come from the store buffer and the compiler, not from per-thread copies of memory

options.text: The JIT can schedule the compiled reader so it races the writer more often, since x86 hardware orders a plain-field handoff by itself
options.says: if the hardware ordered the handoff, no timing could produce published true with payload 0; the JIT reordered the writer's stores

origin.section: The JIT Reorders Too, So x86 Shows a Reordering Its Hardware Doesn't Make

questions.stem: In a rate limiter, an admitting thread sets `admitting = true`, then checks `paused`; a pausing thread sets `paused = true`, then checks `admitting`. Neither may proceed if it sees the other's flag set. A reviewer makes `paused` volatile and leaves `admitting` plain. Which statement about the new version is true?

options.text: Both threads can still read the other's flag as false, since the admitting thread's plain write can reach the other thread only after a lock
options.says: in the one-volatile run the other thread saw the plain write in millions of trials with no lock involved; the failure comes from the plain write and its read swapping

options.text: Both threads can still read the other's flag as false, since the admitting thread's read can still be performed before its plain write
options.says: store buffering needs each thread's write ordered before its own read; with one field plain, that thread's write and read can still swap (sb-half)

options.text: Both threads can no longer read the other's flag as false, since the volatile `paused` can order the admitting thread's plain accesses as well
options.says: one volatile field orders a handoff, not a write-then-read handshake in each thread; the one-volatile run still ended with both reads 0

options.text: Both threads can no longer read the other's flag as false, since the volatile write of `paused` can publish the admitting thread's plain write as well
options.says: a volatile write publishes the writes that come before it in its own thread's program order; the one-volatile run still ended with both reads 0

origin.section: volatile on Every Access That Needs Ordering Rules Out Both Reorderings

questions.stem: A price cache stores `new Quote(symbol, price)` in a plain field; `Quote`'s fields are plain and set in its constructor. Request threads read the field without a lock. A stress test of 200,000,000 reads on an x86 laptop never saw a `Quote` with price 0. Which conclusion is right?

options.text: The cache can be relied on with any JVM, since a constructor's writes complete before the new reference can be stored
options.says: the constructor's writes and the reference store are plain writes to different variables, which may be reordered

options.text: The cache can be relied on with any x86 JVM, since both the JIT and x86 hardware keep a thread's stores in order
options.says: the JIT reordered two plain stores on x86 in the message-passing run; only the hardware keeps stores in order there

options.text: The cache can still fail with another JVM or processor, since the JLS lets a racing reader see the reference before the constructor's writes
options.says: not observed here, but allowed: only final fields come with a guarantee for a racing reader

options.text: The cache can still fail with another JVM or processor, since the JLS lets x86 hardware swap two stores, too rarely for this test to catch
options.says: x86 hardware keeps one core's stores in order (the interpreted message-passing run never showed a swap); the risk the page names is the JIT and weaker processors

origin.section: A Racy Reference May Expose an Object Before Its Constructor's Writes Land

questions.stem: Two workers claim a shared slot: each writes its own `claim` field, then reads the other's, and backs off if it sees a claim. Both fields were volatile; to save cost, a teammate switches every write to `VarHandle.setRelease` and every read to `getAcquire`. Which statement about the new version is true?

options.text: Neither worker can miss the other's claim, since setRelease and getAcquire give volatile's ordering with fewer fences
options.says: volatile adds a total order over all volatile accesses; release/acquire doesn't order a write before a later read

options.text: Neither worker can miss the other's claim, since a setRelease becomes visible to other threads before the writer's next instruction
options.says: a release write can still sit in the store buffer while the writer's next read runs

options.text: Both workers can miss each other's claim, since a getAcquire can complete before the same thread's earlier setRelease is visible
options.says: store buffering with release/acquire ended with both reads 0 in 610,780 trials; only volatile or a full fence ruled it out

options.text: Both workers can miss each other's claim, since setRelease and getAcquire order the accesses to the field they name and no others
options.says: acquire and release order other accesses too (a handoff held); what they don't order is a write followed by a read

origin.section: Acquire/Release Orders a Handoff, Not a Write Followed by a Read
